opus-5.5.text:
What I find really interesting is that these tasks look trivial to us. You put a key in a lock, turn it, push the door open. A child can do it. But for a robot, it combines almost everything that's still hard in manipulation.

First, the precision. A key going into a keyhole has a tolerance of maybe a millimeter or less. Vision alone usually can't get you there. Cameras have calibration error, the hand occludes the keyhole right when you need to see it most, and small errors in the arm add up. So the robot has to do what humans do without thinking: feel its way in. You wiggle the key a bit, you sense when it catches, you adjust. That means using force and touch feedback, not just open-loop planning.

Second, these tasks are contact-rich and multi-stage. You're not moving through free space, you're constantly pushing against the world. You grasp the key in a particular way, insert it, apply torque without dropping it or jamming it, then switch to the handle, then manage the door swinging, which is an articulated object with its own dynamics. Each stage has different physics, and a small mistake early ruins everything after it. That kind of long-horizon, contact-heavy behavior is exactly where many current learning methods break down.

Third, for me personally, there's the question of generalization. Getting a robot to open one specific door in a lab, with lots of engineering, has been possible for a while. The interesting question is whether it can open a door it's never seen, with a different key, a different lock, a stiffer handle. That forces you to think about what the right representation is, what data you need, whether you can learn from human demonstrations or simulation and transfer it to the real world.

So for me these "small" tasks are a really good stress test. If a robot can reliably unlock and open an arbitrary door, it has solved precise perception, compliant control, reasoning over multiple steps, and recovering from failure. Those are the same capabilities you need for almost any useful work in a home. That's why I like them: they're very concrete, very easy to evaluate, you either got the door open or you didn't, and they expose the real gaps in our methods very honestly.

fable-5.1.text:
What fascinates me about unlocking a lock or opening a door is that these look like trivial tasks to us, yet they sit right at the frontier of what robots can do. A person doesn't think about inserting a key. Your fingers feel the resistance, you adjust the angle slightly, you sense when the pin lines up, and you turn. All of that happens below conscious attention. For a robot, every one of those steps is hard, and the difficulty comes from a few places.

First, these tasks are contact-rich. Most of what made robots successful in factories was avoiding contact, or controlling it in a very scripted way. Welding a car body is precise but completely predictable. A lock is different. You are in constant physical contact with an object you can't fully see, the tolerances are sub-millimeter, and the state of the task is hidden inside the mechanism. Vision alone won't tell you whether the key is seated correctly. You need force and tactile sensing, and you need to interpret those signals in real time.

Second, the long tail of variation is enormous. Every door is slightly different. Handles push down, turn, slide. Some doors stick, some swing freely, some are heavy fire doors with closers. A policy that works on one door in the lab and fails on the next one in the hallway is not useful. So these tasks force you to confront generalization honestly. You can't memorize your way through it.

Third, there's the question of recovery. A human who misses the keyhole just tries again, almost without noticing. Robots have historically been brittle. One small error compounds and the whole task fails. Doors and locks are a great benchmark precisely because they punish brittleness and reward systems that can feel their way through uncertainty.

And finally, there's the practical significance. If you want robots to be genuinely useful in homes, hospitals, offices, they have to move through the built environment, and that environment is full of doors and latches and cabinets designed for human hands. A robot that can't open a door is confined to a single room. So this small, almost mundane skill is actually a gateway. Solving it well tells you a lot about whether we've really cracked dexterous manipulation, or whether we're still faking it with carefully arranged demos.

astra-6.text:
What I find especially interesting is that something so ordinary for a person becomes a whole chain of problems for a robot. To unlock a door, it has to locate the keyhole, align the key, insert it, and apply the right amount of force—all while adjusting to tiny differences in position and resistance.

And precision alone isn’t enough. If the key doesn’t turn, should it push a little more, change the angle, or stop? That connection between sensing and action is fascinating to me. Opening a door looks like one simple task, but it really tests whether a robot can respond to the physical world as it changes.

sol-6.1.text: What I find especially interesting is how much complexity is hidden in something that feels effortless to us. To unlock a door, a robot has to align the key, sense contact, apply the right amount of force, and adjust when something doesn’t move as expected. Even opening the door means figuring out how it moves while maintaining a stable grip. It’s a fascinating meeting point between perception, precise control, and responding to uncertainty in the physical world.
